#4910. Muhammad Ali at Home: 10 Photos of the Heavyweight Champion’s Life Outside the Ring

It was a stroke of luck—bad luck—that got Muhammad Ali into the ring for the first time. The Louisville, Kentucky, native was 12 years old when his brand-new bicycle was stolen. The police officer to whom Ali reported the theft happened to own a boxing gym—and became his first coach.

Ten years later, in 1964, Ali, then still known by his birth name, Cassius Clay, became the world heavyweight champion when he defeated reigning titleholder Sonny Liston. The athlete, who earned the nickname “The Greatest,” would go on to win that title two more times, as well as an Olympic gold medal and numerous honors for his civil rights activism and humanitarian work.

There was, of course, another side to the legend: his domestic life. As we gear up for the release of the Prime Video series The Greatest, which explores the prizefighter’s rise to prominence, we’re looking back at photos of Ali in his off-duty hours.

Days after becoming the heavyweight champion, Ali announced his conversion to the Nation of Islam, changed his name, and then relocated to Chicago, where the controversial religion’s headquarters are based. (He later converted to Sunni Islam). In 1967, Ali cited his religious beliefs when he refused to serve in the US Army during the Vietnam War. His boxing license revoked and his championship title stripped, Ali entered a period of exile. He is pictured in his Chicago home the following year, reading a book by Nation of Islam leader Elijah Muhammad. The athlete shared the dwelling with his second wife, Khalilah Camacho-Ali, whom he married at the residence on August 17, 1967. The single-story brick house was in the Avalon Park neighborhood and was a fully furnished gift from the Nation of Islam.

The boxer and his toddler Maryum feeding 10-week-old twins Rasheda and Jamillah in their Philadelphia home.

The couple welcomed a daughter, Maryum, in 1968, and two years later, twins named Rasheda and Jamillah. The newborns are pictured between Ali and Maryum at home in Pennsylvania in this November 1970 photograph. The fighter and his family stayed at the home, in West Philadelphia’s Overbrook Park neighborhood, for about a year. It was later owned by Kobe Bryant’s grandparents.

Ali with fans at his Pennsylvania training camp in August 1974.

Though he soon relocated to New Jersey, Ali would maintain ties to Pennsylvania for decades with his training camp, Fighter’s Heaven. He purchased the Deer Lake property in 1972, the year after the Supreme Court overturned his draft-evasion conviction, allowing him to regain his boxing license. On the land, he custom-built a log gym, a dining hall, several cabins, a mosque, and a courtyard with a large stone fireplace. His training sessions were open to the public; in this August 1974 photo, a group of fans are pictured behind him at the camp. He kept the retreat long after his retirement, selling it in 1997 to martial arts instructor George Dillman. The property is now a tourist destination, complete with a small museum.

Ali at home in Los Angeles before his fight with Larry Holmes.

Ali briefly retired from boxing at age 37 in 1979, but returned the following year to fight Larry Holmes. The boxer poses at his home office in Hancock Park, Los Angeles, in this August 1980 photo, taken about a month before his fight with Holmes.

Ali shoots pool in his Hancock Park house in this 1980 photo.

Ali shows off the game room in his Hancock Park, Los Angeles, home in this 1980 snapshot. Around this period, he started to show early symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, which impacted his athletic ability. He lost the fight to Holmes and went back into retirement.

The boxing champion and his wife Veronica at home in 1982.

In 1981, Ali fought one last time before hanging up his gloves. “I know it’s the end,” he said after losing the fight. “I’m not crazy. After Holmes, I had excuses. I was too light. Didn’t breathe right. No excuses this time. I’m happy. I’m still pretty. I could have a black eye. Broken teeth. Split lips. I think I came out all right for an old man.” Ali stands next to his third wife, Veronica Porché, in front of his Hancock Park dwelling in this photo, taken a few months after his final match.

The Greatest takes a call at home in 1982.

In this photo from the same March 1982 photo shoot, Ali strikes a pose in his opulent Los Angeles living room. The retired boxer had purchased the 14,500-square-foot home in 1979, two years after marrying Porché. The 1916 build, by architect John C. Austin, was an Italian Renaissance mansion complete with seven bedrooms.

The estate featured stained glass window panels designed by Louis Comfort Tiffany (the son of Tiffany & Co. founder Charles Lewis Tiffany) and a stately dining room with intricately carved dark wood and a crystal chandelier, as seen in this October 1985 photo of Ali eating cereal. That year, he and Porché filed for divorce.

Ali outfitted the home with a (packed) trophy room, which he shows off in this 1985 picture. He left the Hancock Park dwelling the following year, when his and Porché’s divorce was finalized. Shortly after, Ali married his fourth wife, Lonnie Williams. As his Parkinson’s disease progressed (he was officially diagnosed in 1984), Williams became Ali’s primary caregiver.

The former fighter has his picture taken by photographer Neil Leifer at home in Arizona’s Paradise Valley.

Ali poses for a photo shoot commemorating his 70th birthday in 2012 at the Arizona home he and Williams shared. That year, he was honored with the Liberty Medal for his humanitarian efforts, which he devoted more time to following his retirement. He was also awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. Ali died in Arizona in 2016 at 74.

#4908. Redwood and Rivian set to expand their EV battery recycling partnership

Redwood Materials and Rivian are expanding their existing EV battery partnership, adding a fresh battery material recycling effort to the EV startup’s Normal, Illinois, vehicle factory and, potentially, other Rivian-owned sites.

As Tesla co-founder JB Straubel’s second act, Redwood Materials had a lot to live up to. Its plan to give used EV batteries a second life as energy storage for public- and private-sector buildings, construction sites, micro-grids, and (sigh) data centers makes plenty of sense, though. Enough sense, anyway, that Rivian decided to put the idea to work as it built out its R2 production line at the former Diamond-Star Mitsubishi plant in Normal. Back in April, the upstart EV brand signed on for 10 MWh worth of energy storage using repurposed Rivian battery packs – but that deal was just the beginning.

The new, expanded partnership between the two companies will see Redwood collect, sort, and recycle Rivian’s battery production scrap materials, putting them safely back into the manufacturing process with minimal waste and at a fraction of the cost of virgin material. What’s more, the new deal will see retired Rivian batteries put to use in other stationary energy projects before eventually recycling some 99% of those batteries’ critical materials (nickel, cobalt, copper, and lithium).

With the recent launch of what is sure to be the more popular, more affordable R2, that’s suddenly a much bigger deal than it might have been last year.

“Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials,” explains Straubel. “Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible, and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keep rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”

Rivian is the latest major EV brand to enter into a formal battery recycling partnership with Redwood, with the list of others including BMW, Ford, Toyota, and Volvo.

#4905. This DC Designer’s Nearly 200-Year-Old Virginia Farmhouse Flourishes With Detail and History

In the foothills of Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains, just minutes from Shenandoah National Park, the town of Sperryville (population: 350) still feels like a well-kept secret. In recent years, it’s attracted the eye of Washington, DC–based designer Melissa Colgan of Melissa Colgan Interiors, who purchased a weekend home there in 2023.

Though born in the Midwest, the designer and her husband, Daniel Schned, moved to DC in 2016 and spent their early years and weekends exploring the surrounding countryside. “One of the areas we fell in love with is Rappahannock County,” she says of discovering its scenic pastures, rolling hills, and grazing cows. “It feels a world away from DC.”

The staircase is covered in Schumacher’s Caterpillar Leaf print and the stair runner is by Sinclair Till. The cloche is custom by Dan Nakamura.

In the family room, the BDDW sofa is upholstered in a Décors Barbares fabric. The side table is from Covesville Antiques and topped with a lamp by Christopher Spitzmiller. The artwork is by Molly van Amerongen.

The fruitwood dining table from 1stDibs is surrounded with chairs by Lorenzo Castillo and upholstered in a fabric by Schumacher. The 1930s chandelier has custom shades covered in a Decors Barbares fabric. The chairs are by Leah O’Connell (left) and Soane. The artwork is by Joshua Perkin.

In 2020, the couple eloped at The Inn at Little Washington and began looking for a vacation home in the area. Three years later, they found a listing for an 1830s farmhouse and barn, which happened to be the former home and office of the county doctor. “It’s a very special house in Sperryville because it’s where the doctor saw all his patients in the early 1900s,” Colgan says.

What began as an 1830s single-room log cabin evolved to include a barn and second story in the 1890s, followed by another addition in the late 1990s. “A lot of the original details were still there,” Colgan says of the 1,200-square-foot residence. “We just wanted to freshen things up a bit.”

In the family living room, the windows, along with the original chink log siding, date to the 1830s. “I wanted to lean into some of the depth that was already there,” Colgan says of her color palette. “That prompted me into the world of deep reds, ochres, and blues.”

In a cozy corner, a Casamidy chair covered in soft mohair flanks a Swedish Gustavian oak secretary from the 1800s.

Colgan solicited the help of DC architect Alexander Smith of Mortar & Thatch. “The thing we aligned with from the very beginning is we didn't want it to feel like a new renovation,” Smith says. “Maybe we slapped on some paint or got new countertops, but we didn’t want it to seem like we were implanting foreign ideas.”

The biggest task was subdividing the single bedroom upstairs to accommodate Colgan’s growing family. At the time, she was pregnant with her now two-year-old daughter. “We basically took down the walls of the one bedroom, made a middle bedroom for our daughter, then eked every inch we could in order to fit a king bed and built-in closets in our room,” she says. The result is a quaint and colorful two-bedroom blueprint, with dappled light dancing through the street-facing windows.

In the pocket-size half bath, an American Federal mahogany mirror broadens the space, which is wrapped in Iksel Mogul Berry Wallpaper by Schumacher and adorned with an oil painting by Jay Harper.

Incorporating open shelves in the kitchen helped maximize storage while enabling the designer to showcase more of the home’s attractive chink log siding. Farrow & Ball’s Terre de Egypte paint accentuates Colgan’s collections of splatterware mugs and vintage objects, like an early-20th-century painter’s palette.

Today, they spend most of their time in the living room downstairs, with its original chink log siding from the 1830s. “The room is so soulful. You just walk in and take a deep breath,” she says. “The thing that came to mind early on was a little Russian country house or dacha. When we first saw the listing, we were in Switzerland, so that was the original seed for the design.”

Drawing from the warmth and depth of the living room’s original pine floors and log siding, Colgan conjured a rich color palette of ochres, reds, and blues with botanical and floral-patterned fabrics that mirrored the pastoral landscape. “We’re surrounded by mountains and flora and fauna, so I wanted the house to reflect that as well.”

A brisbee curtain in Lake August’s flowering Nasturtium fabric adds light and whimsy to the kitchen’s neutral cabinetry.

The kitchen pendants are by Urban Electric. The walls are painted in Dimity and the cabinets are painted Joa’s White, both by Farrow & Ball. The rug is by Matt Camron.

The furnishings are an array of old, new, and local finds from their 1920s French fruitwood dining table to the early American rocking chair salvaged from Ruckersville Antiques. “We didn’t really have anything for this house because the style is so different from our city home, so we had to start from scratch,” Colgan says. Still, the designer is an avid collector and had some pieces sitting in storage like the BDDW sofa, purchased at auction, that’s now in her living room. Currently, it’s upholstered in Décors Barbares’ lively Roses Tchékhonine print, with winged butterflies flitting across a canvas of cobalt and crimson flowers.

In the primary bedroom, every inch mattered. “We did multiple layouts and wanted to make sure the details, finishes, and everything in there was an appropriate scale so things didn’t feel too big or too small for the space,” says Smith. The walls and his-and-her closets are painted in Farrow & Ball’s Pink Ground and Eating Room Red, with Roman shades done in a Lucrezia fabric by Fortuny. An acrylic and ink work on paper by artist Julie Wolfe, which Colgan gave to her husband for their first wedding anniversary, hangs over the bed.

In the sunlit bathroom, blue and white garden tiles from Marble Systems bloom alongside fittings by Waterworks, D Porthault patterned towels, and an antique French mirror, circa 1785.

Other spaces, like the mudroom and laundry located near the home’s side entrance, were made more welcoming and useful, with cupboards dressed in wholesome, hay-colored gingham skirts. Reconfiguring appliances and adding cabinets and open shelving helped optimize the kitchen’s storage and traffic flow. “We were able to inch out so much in such a small space,” Smith says.

Despite its demure size, the house today is a sensory retreat for the couple. “That first Thanksgiving was a real stress test,” Colgan says. The barn in the back, where the doctor kept his horse for making house calls across the county, was renovated by the previous owner to include a kitchenette, an open living room space, and sleeping quarters. “The barn had pigs in it up until the last owner, and he renovated it,” she says. “I’ve since layered in a lot of fabrics and antiques.”

In their daughter’s room, a late-19th-century faux-bamboo pine and bird’s eye maple bed is made up with D Porthault Pink Coeur’s linens and a one-of-a-kind PROJEKTITYYNY Wisteria baby quilt, stitched with Liberty fabrics. The bookshelf is from Crate & Barrel and the walls and windows are covered in Ottoline’s blue and brown Indian Tulip print.

The walls are covered in Caterpillar Leaf by Schumacher and the slipper chair is custom. The Roman shade is a fabric by Antoinette Poisson.

Off the home’s side entry, a laundry and mudroom papered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash design is further brightened thanks to the café curtain and cabinet skirts in a jumbo gingham by Beata Heuman, finished with French grosgrain trim.

Ultimately, however, it was the historic farmhouse where Colgan concentrated her creative energy. “A lot of times people come into these old houses and instead of trying to think carefully about how to make modern life function there, they blow out walls and make everything open,” she says. Instead, she champions her home’s nuanced details, including planks of weathered wood that have patinated over time or the way sunlight shimmers off the 19th-century windows, with their panes of wavy glass. “They are very much not energy efficient,” she says, “but they are absolutely beautiful.”

The custom console is painted in Benjamin Moore’s Van Deusen Blue and the walls are covered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash Spring. The 1960s mirror is from 1stDibs.

On the front porch, a five-piece set by Newell Jacobsen is upholstered in a sky-blue Lisa Fine Madras Performance fabric that complements the painted ceiling, and the neighbor’s vibrant home. “There are some fun houses on our street—the one across the street is yellow,” Colgan says. “I liked the idea of colors out there being a little brighter.”

#4904. The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E gains a standard long-range battery and starts at $40,000

Ford opened orders for the 2027 Mustang Mach-E, which now offers a standard extended-range battery for under $40,000. A new Trail model is also joining the lineup.

Ford’s electric crossover SUV is back for another model year. The 2027 Mustang Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery.

The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-e is available in five trims: Select, Premium, GT, Rally, and a new purpose-built Trail model.

The new 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail is available for a $2,295 package upgrade for the Select eAWD.

According to Ford, the new Trail package is designed to make “outdoor adventures across pavement, gravel, and dirt roads more accessible than ever.”

It features fine-tuned front and rear struts and springs, a Rally-shaped steering rack, 19-inch High Gloss Dark Carbonized Gray Wheels with as-cast graphics, and is 10 mm taller in the front and 15 mm taller in the rear than the base Mach-E.

The 2027 Mustang Mach-E Trail comes with standard 400W, 120V Pro Power Onboard. It’s available as an upgrade for other variants, including the Premium, GT, and Mustang Mach-E Rally.

Select and Premium models use the 88 kWh battery and are available with rear- or all-wheel-drive (eAWD) powertrains. The GT and Rally variants use the 91 kWh battery and are only sold as eAWD models.

Ford’s BlueCruise 1.5 comes standard on the GT and Rally and optional on Select with Tech Pack Lite and Premium with Premium Tech Pack models. The Trail requires the hardware selection at the time of ordering. It cannot be added later.

Meanwhile, the Ford Connectivity Package and Ford Security Package are standard across the entire 2027 lineup.

The base 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Select RWD starts at $39,995. Including the $2,045 destination fee, prices start at $42,040.

While it is a bit more expensive than the 2026 model year, Ford no longer offers the standard-range battery. Ford said a new secondary front motor delivers the same performance as the previous unit but at a lower cost, enabling the lower-priced base RWD model with the extended-range battery.

We're at almost 80,000 miles in our Mach E GT and we'll drive it to 200,000+. It's a blast to drive and we've loved owning it. Feels as solid now as it did day 1.

Bought a set of summer tires at 43k miles. Other than that, and swapping between winter/summer tires, the maintenance cost has been $0.

We don't DC fast charge very often, so the slower L3 charging isn't a big deal for us - but does need improvement IMO.

Previously, the extended-range battery was available, starting at $45,345 on the 2026 Mustang Mach-E.

The extended-range (88 kWh) battery provides an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 320 miles in RWD models. Depending on the configuration, eAWD models offer 300 miles of range. The GT and Rally use the 91 kWh battery, providing 280 miles and 255 miles of range, respectively.

Ford will announce the final EPA-estimated driving range for the Trail model closer to when it goes on sale, expected in the first quarter of 2027.

#4903. The 87 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 17 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4902. Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B

Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”

Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”

Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.

The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”

There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.

Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:

Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.

The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.

Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.

Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.

Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.

If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.

The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.

Rearranging the deck chairs ahead of the merger?

None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.

Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.

The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

#4901. 7 Pendant Lights to Perfect Your Overhead Lighting Scheme (2026)

Sure, recessed lighting serves a functional purpose, but pendant lights are where things get interesting. A quick sweep through any home tour, and you’ll recognize the strategically placed Louis Poulsen above the kitchen island, an Isamu Noguchi in the entryway, and a Herman Miller saucer pendant hovering over the living room that will steal the show. Below are seven pendant light fixtures that set the mood instead of harshening the vibe. We rounded up the best pendant lights for various design personalities, including a vintage-inspired showpiece and a few variations of low-key ambient lighting. Among them are most of the different types of pendant lights you’re likely to come across, with picks for modern minimalists, Belle Époque enthusiasts, and everyone in between.

First developed in 1958, the PH 5 is a classic for a reason. Renowned Danish lighting manufacturer Louis Poulsen designed the iconic pendant with a three-shade system to equally distribute light. While the pendant works for that functional purpose, it also doubles as an unconventional art piece. Choose from a number of monochromatic and multitone colorways, including this steel blue.

Look familiar? That’s because this large pendant, inspired by Noguchi’s Akaris, hangs in many an AD home tour, including above the dining room table in this Japandi-inspired Bay Area home and in the bedroom of this South African–inspired craft home, for example. There are a few reasons why this style of paper lighting is so popular: It goes with everything; it’s affordable; and it adds a sense of levity to the room with its ethereal shape and its soft, warm glow. As lantern pendants go, this option from Design Within Reach is about as low-commitment as they come. It works anywhere you want ambient lighting rather than a spotlight.

Designer pendant lights can cost upwards of $500, but you can pay a fraction of that with finds from Article, a direct-to-consumer furniture store that sells high-quality wares at more palatable prices. That’s certainly the case with the Aino pendant, with matte colorways and a simple angular silhouette that illuminates whatever you’re chef-ing up in your Scandi-style kitchen. The metal cone shade and braided fabric cord make it an easy pick for task lighting over a counter, and if you’re working with a tighter kitchen space, there’s also a mini pendant version for $99 that ships with an LED bulb.

This three-tiered ceiling light from West Elm adds visual texture to blank space, making it a welcome addition to transitional areas in need of personality. A piece like this can also help to add structure to an open plan where the kitchen and dining rooms collide. This piece comes in 26-inch and 32-inch sizes (the larger is a proper large pendant light that can hold its own over a dining table), as well as in hardwired and plug-in options, making it one of the few statement hanging lights you can install without calling an electrician.

Any cold kitchen space dominated by stone and steel fixtures could use a touch of handmade whimsy. Hanging this handwoven rattan pendant over a kitchen island promises to warm up the whole room. Usually, two or three pendant lights hang over a kitchen island; this single shade provides a cozy, welcoming alternative, softening the light rather than spotlighting the countertop, so your mise en place won’t feel so interrogated.

This midcentury Herman Miller pendant, aptly named a saucer for its elliptical shape, is prized by commerce writer Julia Harrison for its retro, Mad Men–esque appeal. Despite the resemblance to our Hay pick above, Miller wasn’t riffing on Noguchi with this pendant: He wanted a Swedish silk-covered pendant he couldn’t justify buying, so he made his own using a sprayed plastic skin originally developed for mothballing Navy ships (whereas the orbital Hay version uses rice paper). The vertical ribbing gives it a shape that seems to be almost expanding as it hangs. Its white shade and chrome hardware make it easily adaptable to many (if not most) design styles.

This lighting fixture brings to mind 10-foot ceilings, Flemish tapestries, and an echoey marble entryway. If you’re lucky enough to have all of the above, this is exactly the sort of pendant your space needs. If not, luckily, the fixture carries that whole vibe on its own, with its cream glass bowl, brass detailing, and a sculpted metal tassel that adds a bit of movement. A vintage-inspired piece like this transforms a more humble hallway into something dignified and scenic.

The new series reunites the True Detective duo for some meta sitcom chaos.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERYONE KNOWS THAT Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are one of the great duos in show business. After meeting and becoming friends on the set of the 1999 comedy film EdTV, the actors began a long friendship, along the way collaborating again for the first season of True Detective, widely considered to be one of the great television shows of all time.

But did you know that in addition to being great friends, the two might also be half-relatives? That’s the premise of Apple TV’s new comedy series Brothers, which reunites the duo on screen for the first time since 2014’s True Detective, and pulls from a bit of very real mythology that the two only relatively recently discovered on their own. “Matthew’s mother, I’d known her 25 years, and she told me, ‘I knew your father.’ You know, like, with the ellipses: ‘I knew… your father’” Harrelson told Variety. “She tells me, and I’m thinking, ‘What’s behind this story?’ And then I find out they weren’t just friends—there was a little more to it.”

Brothers, in turn, stars McConaughey and Harrelson as fictional versions of themselves exploring this possibility. Think of it as the meta-nature of Curb Your Enthusiasm, combined with the goofiness of a family sitcom like Schitt’s Creek or Malcolm in the Middle, and, of course, the star power of True Detective.

Now, just because they made the show doesn’t mean that McConaughey believes the story. “Woody thinks he knows that we’re brothers, and it’s not that I don’t want to know—I don’t believe it,” McConaughey told Variety at the show’s premiere. “My mom’s the one who started this whole damn thing, by saying ‘I knew… your father… with the long pause after that. Even my five-year-old son understood the innuendo of what that meant.”

So, are the A-listers actually brothers? You figure they could just take a DNA test and figure out once and for all. But for now, that doesn’t seem to be in the cards. “I’ve been wanting to, but he refuses,” Harrelson told The Hollywood Reporter. McConaughey then added that maybe that could change in the future—but he’s a little frightened about what it could mean. “I’ll probably come around to it,” he said. “If it’s true, I’ve got a lot to unpack. If it’s not true, he’s not going to be near as fun to hang out with.”

There’s a lot to figure out for these two. But in the meantime, why not see how fictional Matthew and Woody handle it? Below, we’ve got all the information to make sure you don’t miss an episode of Apple TV’s Brothers.

The final episode of Brothers season 1 will officially come out on Wednesday, November 4. But as with all Apple TV shows, it'll release a bit early the night prior. So if you're eager, keep an eye out for the next episode on the evening of Tuesday, November 3.

The debut season of Brothers will run for eight episodes, with episodes rolling out on a weekly basis, the first seven of which have now aired. That means there’s still one more week—and one episodes of Matthew and Woody’s brotherly (or not-so-brotherly) chaos—remaining in the show’s first season.

#4891. Fortescue is using KUKA welding robots to handle 6 MW charging cables [video]

Humanoid robots aren’t ready to juice up the massive, 240-tonne electric haul trucks Fortescue is putting to work in Australia’s punishing Pilbara. Instead, the company is using specially modified and massively powerful automotive assembly-line robots from KUKA to wrangle the massive cables needed to deliver a mind-bending 6 MW of power to its trucks’ batteries.

While Chinese car brands capable of 2 MW “flash charging” are making headlines these days, Fortescue and Liebherr have been quietly working together to develop a 6MW charging system for their massive, ultra heavy-duty mining rigs since 2024 – but details about how the process actually works have been scarce.

Until now, that is. In a new video released by the company earlier this month, Fortescue explains how it delivers what amounts a controlled lightning bolt into the battery of its specially developed, 264 (short) ton Liebherr T264E electric haul truck. And, because the massive, liquid-cooled copper cables are too big, too heavy, and too dangerous for any human to handle, of course they’re using robots to get the job done.

“The challenge with a six megawatt charger is that nobody makes these, and therefore nobody makes a lot of the components, either,” says a Fortescue representative, in the video. “So, we’ve had to take systems and subsystems from different industries were using industrial robots that would normally be used for welding in a car factory.”

Fortescue was able to develop and refine its KUKA robots with help from a $10 million (AUD) grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), which were earmarked to help the company develop a six megawatt (MW) fast charger test unit and support its ultimate goal of achieving true net zero operations by 2030.

“Leveraging our world-class capability in battery and charging solutions from motorsport, the fast chargers have been developed for the challenging conditions of the Pilbara,” explained Fortescue Zero’s then-Chief Executive Officer, Ellie Coates, when the grant was announced in 2024. “Equipped with robotic connection options, they will be able to power Fortescue’s future 240-tonne Liebherr T 264 battery electric trucks in just 30 minutes.”

No need to reinvent the wheel, Cruise ship and other large vessels have ben using shore power for years when docked. these typical range from 7 MW to 16 MW, just borrow their tech, a overhead crane to lift the cable and an operator to plug it on

The Liebherr T264E packs an impossibly large 3.2 MWh (3,200 kWh) battery pack – the equivalent capacity of about 40 road-going Tesla Model Y crossovers – to put that 30 minute spec into context. You can check out the company’s official video, below, then let us know what you think of the 6 MW charging robots in the comments.

#4889. Kia’s EV6 GT beat out the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 in a German EV comparison test

Kia’s electric sports car beat out the Tesla Model Y Performance and BYD’s Sealion 7 in a recent comparison test by the German magazine Auto Motor und Sport, ranking first overall.

It wasn’t a German brand or a Chinese one. It wasn’t even the Tesla Model Y Performance. Kia’s electric sports car, the EV6 GT, took first place in a recent high-performance EV test in Germany, the heart of Europe.

The comparison test, held by German auto magazine Auto Motor und Sport, evaluated five high-performance EVs across seven categories: body, safety, comfort and convenience, powertrain, driving performance, environmental friendliness, and running costs.

The EV6 GT ranked first overall with 585 points, 9 points ahead of the Tesla Model Y Performance, which took second with 576 points.

The Zeekr 7GT ranked third with 569 points, followed by the Polestar 4 Coupe Dual Motor with 531 points, and the BYD Sealion 7 AWD Excellence, which ranked fifth with 508 points.

Kia’s electric sports car took the top spot in three of the seven categories: safety, powertrain, and driving performance. In the safety category, the EV6 GT scored highest for its superior braking and high-speed stability.

The EV6 GT earned praise in the powertrain category, boasting up to 650 horsepower and 770 Nm of torque from its dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain.

In the driving performance category, Kia’s electric sports car scored 20 points higher (96 points) than the Tesla Model Y Performance in second (76 points).

According to Auto Motor und Sport, the Kia EV6 GT took first place overall in the comparison test due to its “outstanding driving performance.”

Performance is one thing, but it also stands out with fun features, including Virtual Gear Shift. Borrowed from the Hyundai IONIQ 5 N, the feature simulates the feeling and sounds of a six-speed paddle-operated transmission.

Kia overhauled the interior for the newest model with its new connected car Navigation Cockpit (ccNC) infotainment system.

The new system includes dual 12.3″ navigation and driver display screens in a curved panoramic setup.

Kia’s electric sports car can sprint from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds. It uses a new 84 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

With 800V fast-charging capabilities, the Kia EV6 GT can recharge from 10% to 80% in as little as 18 minutes.

In Germany, the new Kia EV6 GT starts at 69,990 euros ($78,000). The Tesla Model Y Performance, on the other hand, starts at 63,970 euros in Germany. It offers a WLTP range of up to 360 miles (580 km) and accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds.

Which high-performance EV would you drive? The Kia EV6 GT or the Tesla Model Y Performance? Let us know in the comments.

Unfortunately, Kia said it was discontinuing the EV6 GT in the US “until further notice” earlier this year.

#4886. New Jersey may finally reverse its draconian e-bike law after massive backlash

New Jersey lawmakers are already looking to walk back one of the country’s most controversial e-bike laws, just months after the sweeping new regulations took effect and sparked widespread backlash from riders, bicycle shops, and advocacy groups.

A newly introduced bill, S4830, sponsored by State Senator Raj Mukherji, would remove licensing, registration, and insurance requirements for low-speed electric bicycles with motors rated at 750W or less and a maximum motor-powered speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). This includes Class 1 and Class 2 electric bicycles.

The proposal would essentially restore bicycle-like treatment for these two classes of e-bikes, importantly including throttle-equipped models that make up the majority of e-bikes sold in the state and more broadly in the US, while maintaining stricter requirements for faster and more powerful electric bicycles.

The move comes after New Jersey’s previous governor, Phil Murphy, signed a sweeping e-bike law in January following several tragic crashes involving young riders.

That legislation, which took full effect in July, eliminated the state’s previous three-class e-bike framework and introduced licensing and registration requirements for all electric bicycles, including ordinary low-speed commuter models. Throttle-equipped and faster e-bikes also faced insurance requirements.

As we previously reported, New Jersey bicycle shops experienced devastating sales declines after the law took effect, with some reporting drops of 20% to 90%. Several businesses were forced to lay off employees, downsize, or even close entirely as e-bike sales and usage plummeted.

Meanwhile, riders faced confusing new requirements that made e-bikes considerably less accessible, which was particularly impactful for lower-income residents, people with disabilities, and those who rely on electric bicycles for daily transportation.

I own a Class 3 e-bike, but I also acknowledge that with its potential assisted speed of 28mph it's of a different breed than Class 1/2 bikes -- that's just too fast in crowded bike lanes or shared use paths.

The first priority should be to target reckless riding by anyone, and illegal bikes should be confiscated if they're involved.

The original law was intended to improve safety, but critics argued that it largely punished responsible riders instead of addressing the growing problem of high-powered electric motorcycles masquerading as bicycles. Only responsible riders actually registered their bikes as required by law, while others were deterred from cycling, and the hooligan riders who often gave e-bikes a bad name continued to ride illegally.

After all, requiring someone riding a 20 mph (32 km/h) commuter e-bike to obtain a driver’s license and register their bicycle does little to address reckless riding on machines capable of highway speeds.

The newly proposed legislation appears to acknowledge that distinction, offering a more targeted approach that could preserve reasonable safety regulations without making ordinary e-bike ownership unnecessarily complicated.

S4830 still needs to work its way through the legislature before becoming law, but for New Jersey’s struggling e-bike industry, it’s a promising sign that lawmakers may finally be listening. It is still widely argued that requiring electric bicycles from 21-28 mph (32-45 km/h) to require a driver’s license and registration is overly burdensome, but at least the state appears to be moving back toward the right direction.

#4884. They’ve Taken on Clayface, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Star Trek. But Can They Survive Each Other?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing are some of the busiest comic book writers in the business—and their deep, complex, and long-standing friendship and working relationship is the biggest reason why.

RELATIONSHIPS ARE HARD. Interpersonal dynamics of any sort require work to maintain—Ben Affleck took a lot of shit for saying his marriage was work, but he was right. A myriad of different factors can destabilize a dynamic between people at any given moment: ego, money, miscommunication, and on the list goes.

Unless you’re Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing.

The comic writing duo, collectively and colloquially known as “Hivemind,” have worked on major properties including, but certainly not limited to, Captain America, Guardians of the Galaxy, Star Trek, and Thunderbolts. That’s not to mention their creator-owned work, like the new horror comic, You’ll Never Leave This Place Alive, which is akin to Marvel’s Runaways meets M. Night Shyamalan’s The Village. And right now, their work on the 2022 one-shot Batman: One Bad Day: Clayface, is part of the DNA that makes up Clayface—the latest production from James Gunn’s DC Studios and the current #1 movie in America. These are the kinds of projects that most writers would kill to be a part of. And, at every step, this pair has done it together.

In a profession where it often feels like a Battle Royale-style competition to land a paid gig, how and why do these two decide to work together?

The answer dates back to 2005, when the pair met at the University of Southern California’s famed film school. Lanzing remembers being on his very first film set and passing by a sound guy, David Server, talking about the Avengers. After doubling back and clarifying if he was, indeed, talking about the comic, the pair hit it off. Not long after, Lanzing went over to Server’s place to hang out, where he met Kelly, who was Server’s roommate. “We met briefly and became friendly,” Lanzing says. “I was definitely—let’s say—a little more hubristic back then,” Kelly states. “I think I was a little bit high on my own supply and wasn’t really quite as engaging with other folks as much.” Kelly went off to Ireland to study abroad and “came back and discovered that this guy, [Lanzing], was still in our lives. I really thought it was going to be a short, summer fling.”

The trio would pile in a PT Cruiser lovingly nicknamed “The Beast,” because it would “growl anytime you tried to gas it” and trek down to local comic book shops Golden Apple or Meltdown to pick up new issues for the week. The trio would then go to a greasy pizza place, read their books, and talk about them. “Because we were all film students, we’re breaking apart the story,” Kelly says. “We were really doing our best to effectively just be passionate nerds within the space. Once you spend enough time with someone and see their real passion for something, it's hard not to start to bond. Once you start to see that passion in someone's eyes and understand what they care about, that's how real relationships are built.”

In a way, Kelly’s relationship with Server developed as a Step Brothers-esque “Did we just become best friends” moment. But his relationship with Lanzing had more of the slow-burn nature of a courting.

“It genuinely was,” Kelly confirms. “Absolutely.”

If hanging out and talking shop was the getting-to-know-one-another phase of their relationship, the consummation, as it were, came out of shared vulnerability. The two ended up in a writing group, sharing material back and forth. That’s when they finally read one another’s work, and their perspective shifted. Kelly, who had come to USC from small town roots in both Hawaii and Washington state without much of a plan before the screenwriting program took him in, was similarly moved by Lanzing’s work. “I'm realizing the story he wrote was my experience, he says. “This is a brother, not a foe. Embrace him like a brother. From that moment on, that respect changed the dynamic of our relationship.”

The pair spent more and more time together, especially after they graduated and took a road trip to Lollapalooza to see Radiohead—which Kelly wryly describes as “pots and pans being tossed down the stairs music”—where their respect for one another grew. “I have so much respect for who he is as a creator, " Kelly says. “It's almost like they say, Don't meet your heroes, but it's like, I kind of just get to hang out with one of my heroes all the time.” Lanzing quickly chimes in, saying, “ I just had never met somebody who thought the way Collin did . . . I learned pretty early, not as a writing partner, but as a friend, he filled in a lot of my gaps.”

In those early days, the pair didn’t always have the language to express the depths of their friendship to one another, with both agreeing it was easier to pour that into the work and have it manifest there.

“We were able to have that rich emotional relationship without saying those words exactly because we were able to funnel it all through our characters,” Kelly adds. “We were almost forced by the fact that we had pledged our careers to each other. We were like, the only way we're going to get through this life is together, making beautiful stories together, making things that are tragic and real and sincere. That necessitates us opening up and being real and tragic and sincere with each other in a way that's like, whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, this is just for the story, man.”

THE AFOREMENTIONED LOLLAPALOOZA trip turned out to be beneficial not only in furthering the pair’s friendship, but giving them a real foot in the door in Hollywood. As they drove from Los Angeles to Chicago, the boys started riffing on story ideas, eventually hitting on their shared love of Akira Kurosawa movies and Japanese culture. On the road, they put together an outline for a movie called Sundown about seven samurai defending a town from Gaki, aka Japanese vampires. “Ultimately, it's about this guy having to kill his best friend,” Lanzing says. “We didn’t really realize we were writing a lot of the early parts of our relationship into the script.”

By the time the trip back to LA concluded, the duo thought Sundown was in good-but-not-great shape. Kelly had a deal with William Morris, and brought the script to his agent there with the understanding that any sale involving the story was now a package deal. While the movie ultimately never got made, it made enough of an impression to get them recurring work, even as the industry shifted in real time, often being tapped to work on web series, which became all the rage after the 2008 financial crisis.

The two worked part-time on storytelling while holding full-time jobs. That schedule meant they’d get together for face-to-face working sessions on Thursday and all day Sunday. “Our wives, our friends, everybody had to accept the fact that, look, if you want Jack or Collin on [those days], you don't get them,” Kelly says.

With such a complicated working arrangement, the possibility of not working as a duo did come up. At one point, Kelly took a chance to co-write an animation with another writer friend, but the production ended up spanning six different time zones. Fundamentally, the project was messing and began taking a toll on Kelly, to the point where it finally came to a head.

“It genuinely is one of the only times I’ve gotten angry at Collin,” Lanzing adds. “That’s the one time I’ve ever had to deploy it in our relationship because it had literally gotten to the point where it was like, he’s disappearing. Not just into this project but into himself.”

Lanzing found it to be the “scariest” moment in their entire relationship. “I think that is legit one of the first times we were ever really emotionally vulnerable with another,” he says. “The crazy thing is, I think it actually brought us closer together.”

“Oh, yeah,” Kelly interjects. “I was scream crying.”

“We lost it at each other and were able to put it back together,” Lanzing says, picking the thread back up. “I think it taught us both, like, okay, we can do this.”

A FEW YEARS ago, DC Comics published a series of Batman-related one-shots. The series, titled “One Bad Day,” draws inspiration from Alan Moore, Brian Bolland, and John Higgins’ seminal The Killing Joke story. In the story, the Joker rolls out his MO, a fitting bit of text that’s become totemic within comic book lore: “All it takes is one bad day to reduce the sanest man alive to lunacy. That’s how far the world is from where I am. Just one bad day.”

The one-shots featured a handful of stories, all told from the point of view of a Batman villain. Kelly and Lanzing’s story, drawn by Xermanico, follows the Basil Karlo version of Clayface, who is on the verge of a breakout role and slowly descends into madness as he kills more and more people in the film industry to get what he wants. It’s also clearly one of the main sources of inspiration for the DCU’s new body horror film Clayface, which released earlier this month to the excitement of DC fans (and landing at the top of the box office). The film follows a version of Clayface named Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) and his quest for continued fame on the silver screen (even with plenty of body mutations and murders coming along the way).

Kelly says that DC reached out to them specifically because of their Hollywood background—and thought that would be perfect for Clayface. “Talk about taking our trauma and doing our therapy—that book is taking all the pain that we've had and expressing it through the character and taking him through something really genuinely emotional and horrifying,” Kelly says. “And it has nothing to do with being a Clayface.”

But for both men, the book is another kind of cautionary tale. It’s what could have happened to them if they hadn’t found one another. “[Basil] kills and impersonates his supposed best friend,” Lanzing says. “That's the pivot point. That's the thing that makes it not Collin and I's story. Rather than look at the other guy and be like, I want the jobs you have, I want the opportunities you have, I want the talent you have, I want the ideas you have, I want the life you have, I want the face you have. Rather than doing any of that, what we did was we said, What if we take the monetary sacrifice involved in splitting that fifty-fifty, but then do it together and make an alliance that doesn't break, that doesn't lead to one of us stuffing the other one in the back of a car? Does that lead to a better outcome? “At this point, we’re getting to the part of the summit that seems like it led to a better outcome.”

Based on the expansive depth and breadth of their work, the answer is a resounding yes. But in how the two men talk about one another, and their friendship, and what they’ve meant to one another, even without creating together, it’s the kind of relationship anyone would love to have. A perfect partnership where each brings out the best in the other, resulting in something that transcends and goes beyond—even if maintaining and cultivating that relationship can sometimes get tricky or rocky, it’s worth it. Being in a foxhole with someone else is always going to be better than doing it alone.

#4881. The Man Behind Fashion’s Most Dazzling Spectacles Turns His Attention to the Art of Light

For as long as he can remember, Alexandre de Betak has been entranced by light. As a 10-year-old, he rewired his Paris bedroom so that visitors had to be buzzed in, greeted by shifting colored lights. He went on to found Bureau Betak, a set design agency that transformed the runway with its megawatt spectacles for clients like Dior, Gucci, Jacquemus, and Fendi. De Betak estimates that he produced “thousands” of fashion shows—including Saint Laurent’s spring-summer 2020 ready-to-wear extravaganza, for which he bathed the Eiffel Tower in golden light, and installations for Rodarte featuring fluorescent and neon tubes.

A new truss light sculpture by Alexandre de Betak, seen here in a 17th-century Swedish castle

Now, de Betak, who sold his company in 2021, is turning the spotlight on his own creative practice. On November 5, he opened his first solo exhibition of artworks at Salon 94 in New York. The electronically programmed Truss Light Sculptures are inspired by the scaffolding and fixtures of his early runway shows and in some cases literally made from them. “That equipment is old-fashioned now, but I wanted to honor it,” de Betak says. “And I liked the irony that I spent so much energy over the years trying to hide it.”

On view at Salon 94’s Upper East Side town house through December 19, the exhibit presents two series. In the gallery’s contemporary space, the first is composed of freestanding and wall-mounted aluminum structures fitted with LED bulbs. The upstairs Stone Room, a historic space with Caen stone plaster walls and arched windows, is the backdrop for a second series of versions in bronze. To make them, de Betak had a French foundry recast each part down to the smallest screw by hand, a process that sometimes required more than 20 molds.

A pair of wall-mounted sculptures in aluminum

The light sculptures, which vary from sconce-like creations to hulking constructions out of a sci-fi movie, have a sly sense of humor and a human quality. This is especially true when they come to life, thanks to a remote-control-operated system that activates light sequences that glow, sparkle, thrum, or react to ambient noise, “whether a whisper,” de Betak says, “or extremely loud music.” For these effects, he drew on his stage work, where he was renowned for cueing, or choreographing, light and sound. “I’m interested in the ephemeral nature of what this equipment was made to show—whether a fashion show or a ballet,” he says. “At a moment when everything is virtual, I think it’s more important than ever to create things that produce a live emotion.”

Salon 94’s founder Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn observes that de Betak’s sculptures are equally powerful switched on or off. Unlit they remind her of David Smith artworks or Russian constructivism. Lit, and with synced sound, they evoke the theatricality of stage performers. “Alex has spent his career building structures that disappear into someone else’s spectacle,” she says. “Here, the structure is the whole point.”

#4877. How to Organize a Kitchen Pantry in 6 Easy Steps, According to Experts

A pantry is among the most hardworking areas of the home, but without proper skills, it can also turn into the most cluttered. Learning how to organize a kitchen pantry like a pro requires a pro, so we tapped expert organizers to share their best pantry organization tips. Ahead, you’ll find a step-by-step guide to organizing your pantry—and keeping it that way. The process includes decluttering expired items, grouping pantry staples by category, deciding what to place on upper and lower shelves, and utilizing food storage containers and labeled bins. Whether you have a spacious walk-in pantry or you’re working with limited shelf space, use these pantry organization ideas to maximize vertical space, function, and style.

Start by removing everything from your pantry. “As you are taking the items out, take note of expiration dates and toss anything that is past its best by date, that is stale, or is no longer edible,” says Megan Barnhart, a professional organizer and founder of Barnhart Home. Since the pantry is rarely empty, take the opportunity to deep-clean it—wipe pull-out shelves, wash pantry storage vessels, and sweep the floor. You can also use this time to place liners or contact paper on the shelves. “Liners prevent damage to the wood and paint and make future clean-ups so much easier,” says Catherine Benson, a cleaning and organization aficionado based in Lexington, Kentucky.

Removing everything from the pantry will help you survey what you have in order to organize it better.

Before you return everything into the pantry, group items by category. There are several ways to do this, and experts recommend choosing the method that best suits you. One idea is to group like items together. “Think of your pantry as your own personal grocery store—canned goods together, pastas together, baking ingredients together,” Barnhart shares.

Another option is to categorize items by how you shop and plan meals. “If you shop with specific meals in mind and like to meal plan, group those ingredients together; for example, create a dinner zone that includes individual categories or bins such as pasta, grains, and soup,” says Lisa Eckerle, a professional organizer and owner of The Designer Organizer. If you shop by stocking up on pantry goods, categories like canned goods, baking supplies, and condiments may make more sense. “We normally use a hybrid approach for most of our clients, creating zones based on activity and categories within the zones based on food type,” Eckerle shares.

Once you’ve organized your categories, you might want containers to hold them. But before purchasing any storage vessels, measure pantry shelves, noting their width, depth, and height. Barnhart and Eckerle recommend incorporating the following storage solutions to maximize space and add style.

Risers are one of Barnhart’s favorite ways to store canned goods. “It makes it much easier to see the canned items in the back as well as what is in the front, and I feel it also helps avoid over-buying or repurchasing because you can see what you actually have,” she says.

Turntables are a must-have for pro organizers. “With all L-shaped pantries, we always start by placing turntables in most of the corners; these help maximize that space, avoid food getting lost or spoiled in the back, and create a cohesive visual,” Eckerle says. She notes they also work well on pantry shelves above eye level.

Consider containers and other tools to help store items in your pantry more effectively.

Turntables are great for oils and vinegars, sauces, condiments, broths, and spices. “If you have items you use daily, like nut butters, honey, and spreads that do not require refrigeration, consider putting those items on their own lazy Susan as well; it makes it easy to grab what you need and also makes it easy to clean up small spills and drips because they are contained to the lazy Susan,” Barnhart says.

Barnhart suggests using beautiful baskets or clear containers to group together things like snacks and dry goods. “This contains the items so they are not spilling out onto the shelves or floor and it is also much more aesthetically appealing as well,” Barnhart says.

One of Eckerle’s favorite recent hacks are wire cooling racks on the interior bottom of wooden storage bins. “By adding a plastic shelf liner under the cooling rack for easy cleaning, we created a unique fruit bin that was able to match the rest of the pantry’s decor and still store the fruit correctly with proper airflow,” she shares.

Now it’s time to add everything back into the pantry. “The most-reached-for categories should be near the door or center, with back stock and lesser-used category items placed in the back or the sides,” Eckerle says. She suggests putting meal-related items in the most accessible location, especially breakfast items, so they’re easy to grab when you’re in a rush.

Avoid storing seldom-used or heavy, small appliances on the top shelf or floor. “To prevent injury, damage, and frustration, those items should be stored between knee and shoulder height,” Eckerle says. Additionally, consider at what height you want each category. For example, “whether you want items out of reach of young children or dogs, or accessible and at eye level for children,” Eckerle says.

Keep things you grab often towards the front, while less-used items can go in the back.

“I am a big fan of labeling in the pantry—it helps systems stay in place when everyone knows what goes where and where to put it back,” Barnhart says. A label maker works great for this, but even stickers and sharpies will do.

Once you know how to organize a kitchen pantry, it’s important to maintain it. Eckerle recommends lightly resetting the pantry after every grocery haul. Additionally, she advises scheduling a day each quarter for a thorough pantry reset. “Re-check expiration dates, dispose of open food, and throw away or donate the items/categories that are no longer on your menu,” she says. You can also use this time to consider any seasonal menu changes that may impact how you organize your pantry. “Depending on the season, you may purchase different ingredients or cook different types of meals,” says Shweta Thota, a lifestyle content creator and Intel hardware engineer based in Sacramento. “This may require rearranging your pantry to accommodate seasonal items.” For example, in the winter, you may want to have a setup that works for more canned goods.
